Unequal heating
Regional climate

distractorRationale.0: Ocean currents are named as a second, separate layer that adds to the difference between the two posts, not the cause of the wind belts themselves.
distractorRationale.2: Regional climate is the overall pattern the passage is trying to explain, the effect of these mechanisms, not the cause of the wind belts.

items.quote: Unequal heating across the planet drives global wind belts.
items.explain: The passage names unequal heating across the planet as the direct cause of the global wind belts that carry moisture toward Cairn Bay and dry out crossing the land toward Sable Flats.  Ocean currents are introduced afterward as a separate mechanism, and regional climate is the overall pattern these mechanisms together produce.

items.stem: Based on the ten-year averages, which post would most likely support crops that need a steady, narrow range of temperatures year-round?
choices: Sable Flats, since its winter low of twenty-eight degrees is close to freezing.
Cairn Bay, since its ocean current keeps its temperature swings much smaller than Sable Flats' swings.
Sable Flats, since it receives less rainfall and therefore steadier weather overall.
Neither post shows any meaningful difference in temperature swing.

distractorRationale.0: A cold winter low by itself does not describe a narrow, steady range.  Sable Flats posts the wider sixty-eight-degree swing between its seasons, not the steadier one.
distractorRationale.2: The tables show rainfall and temperature swing as two separate measurements.  Less rain does not translate into a steadier temperature range; Sable Flats posts the wider swing of the two posts.
distractorRationale.3: The tables report a real, sizable difference, a sixty-eight-degree swing at Sable Flats against a thirty-three-degree swing at Cairn Bay, roughly double.

items.explain: Cairn Bay's ten-year table posts a thirty-three-degree swing between summer and winter, roughly half of Sable Flats' sixty-eight-degree swing, and the passage ties that steadiness directly to an ocean current that keeps the coastal water within a narrow temperature range all year, making Cairn Bay the better fit for crops that need steady conditions.

items.stem: Which term names "what is happening outside the window this morning," as opposed to a pattern averaged over years?
choices: climate
front
weather
air mass

distractorRationale.0: Climate is the passage's own term for the pattern averaged over years, the opposite of what is happening outside the window on one particular morning.
distractorRationale.1: A front is the meeting point of two air masses, a cause of a single weather event, not the general word for today's conditions outside the window.
distractorRationale.3: An air mass is a huge body of air with its own temperature and moisture, one piece of the weather mechanism, not the general term for today's conditions.

items.explain: The passage defines weather directly as what is happening outside the window this morning, in deliberate contrast to climate, the pattern averaged over years, the same distinction Tile 3's field manual sets up with front and air mass, two different vocabulary words for two different pieces of the mechanism.

items.stem: A third post sits at the same latitude as Sable Flats and Cairn Bay, but far inland with no coastal current anywhere nearby.  Based on the passage's own explanation, would this new post most likely resemble Sable Flats or Cairn Bay?
choices: Cairn Bay, since every post at the same latitude eventually reports a similar climate.
Cairn Bay, since inland posts always receive more ocean-carried moisture than coastal posts.
Neither post, since latitude is the only factor the passage says matters.
Sable Flats, since being far from the ocean means no current and no ocean-carried moisture to moderate its temperature or add rainfall.

distractorRationale.0: The passage's whole point is that shared latitude guarantees neither post a similar climate; Sable Flats and Cairn Bay share a latitude and still report very different conditions.
distractorRationale.1: The passage explains the opposite: wind loses its ocean-picked-up moisture the farther it travels over dry land, so an inland post receives less of that moisture, not more.
distractorRationale.2: The passage names position relative to the ocean, wind belts, and ocean currents as the real mechanisms behind the difference, explicitly stating that latitude alone does not decide a post's climate.

items.explain: The passage explains Sable Flats' climate through its distance from open water: no ocean current to moderate its temperature swings and a wind belt that has already dropped most of its moisture crossing hundreds of miles of dry land before arriving.  A third inland post with no nearby current would share that same lack of moderating mechanisms, making it resemble Sable Flats rather than the coastal Cairn Bay.

items.stem: Match each climate pattern to the mechanism the passages say causes it.
rowLabels: Cairn Bay's temperature swings only thirty-three degrees across the year
Sable Flats' temperature swings sixty-eight degrees across the year
Cairn Bay averages forty-two inches of rain a year
Sable Flats averages only nine inches of rain a year
colLabels: A current keeps the coastal water in a narrow temperature range all year
No current moderates the post, so its land surface heats and cools fast
The wind still carries its ocean-picked-up moisture when it reaches the coast
The wind has already dropped most of its moisture crossing hundreds of miles of dry land
items.explain: Each pattern traces back to a specific, named mechanism: an ocean current moderates Cairn Bay's temperature, Sable Flats has no such current to moderate its own land-heated swings, and the same wind belt arrives moist at the coast but dry at Sable Flats after crossing hundreds of miles of land.  Matching a pattern to the wrong post's mechanism is exactly the confusion this table is built to catch.

partA.stem: What is the real cause of the colony's dropping chick survival rate, according to the record?
choices: The chicks now hatch weeks before the herring, their one food source, arrive.
The colony has been laying fewer eggs every year.
The herring have stopped arriving at Halyard Point entirely.
The nesting date itself, no matter when it falls, causes lower survival.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: In the first logged season, the colony's first eggs came on April seventh.
The herring's arrival date has held near April twenty-first every season.
The colony's chicks now hatch weeks before their food source even arrives.
It was never the nesting date by itself.

distractorRationale.1: This sentence is about when the eggs appear, not how many eggs the colony lays.  The record never reports a falling egg count.
distractorRationale.2: This sentence says the herring's arrival date has held steady near April twenty-first, which means they still arrive every season, just on their own schedule.
distractorRationale.3: The record states the opposite directly: it was never the nesting date by itself that mattered.

items.explain: The record's own closing description names the real cause: the colony's chicks now hatch weeks before the herring, their one food source, even arrive, a reversal from the colony's early seasons, when the herring were already there and settled in.  Each wrong choice either invents a detail the record does not report or contradicts its own stated conclusion.

partA.stem: Why has the colony's nesting date drifted earlier while the herring's arrival date has stayed almost the same?
choices: Terns respond to warming spring air and water, while herring respond to a slower-changing ocean-temperature clock far out at sea.
Terns and herring both respond to the exact same signal, so both dates should have shifted together.
The herring have simply chosen to arrive later every year on purpose.
The terns' nesting date is fixed by the calendar and cannot actually change.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: That is twenty-eight days earlier than the colony's first logged year.
Their bodies respond once conditions cross a warm mark, and thirty years of warming have pulled that mark earlier.
The herring's arrival date has held near April twenty-first every season.
That clock runs slower than the coastal air the terns respond to.

distractorRationale.1: This sentence describes the terns' own signal, the spring air and water warming past a threshold, which is a different, faster-changing cue than the herring's ocean-temperature clock.
distractorRationale.2: The record says the herring's arrival date has held near the same date every season, which is the opposite of choosing to arrive later.
distractorRationale.3: This sentence reports the nesting date moving twenty-eight days earlier over thirty seasons, which directly shows the date can and did change.

items.explain: The passage names two separate clocks: terns respond to spring air and water warming past a threshold, a fast-moving signal, while herring time their arrival by ocean temperature far out at sea, a clock that runs slower than the coastal air the terns respond to, so the two dates have drifted apart instead of moving together.  Each wrong choice either merges the two clocks or misreads which date actually shifted.

partA.stem: Why does Network Command treat the carbon dioxide and fuel-use trends as signs of a steady, human-linked cause rather than normal weather bouncing around?
choices: Both numbers climbed by close to the same amount every single year for ten years without ever dropping back.
The temperature line also climbed by the exact same amount every year, just like the other two.
Carbon dioxide and fuel use are measured at only one station, so they cannot be compared to anything.
The carbon dioxide line dropped back to normal levels several times over the ten years.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Every station on the network logs its local temperature.
Some years rose sharply.
Not one of the past ten years has dropped back.
That climb has stayed steady, year after year.

distractorRationale.1: This sentence is actually about the temperature line, described elsewhere as bouncing, some years rising sharply and one year barely rising at all, not climbing by the same amount every year.
distractorRationale.2: The passage describes carbon dioxide and fuel-use data gathered network-wide, across every station, not from just one location.
distractorRationale.3: The passage says the opposite: that climb has stayed steady, year after year, without a single year dropping back.

items.explain: Network Command draws the distinction directly: a signal that bounces up and down, like the temperature line, points to short-term natural causes, while a signal that climbs the same steady amount every year without ever reversing, like the carbon dioxide and fuel-use lines together, points to a steady, ongoing cause instead.  Each wrong choice either misassigns the bouncing pattern or denies the steady climb the report describes.

partA.stem: How does the network-wide warming pattern explain Halyard Point's own local mystery?
choices: A warmer average is why Halyard Point's spring keeps arriving earlier than the colony's food supply can follow.
The warming pattern has nothing to do with Halyard Point, since its mystery is only about its colony's food source, not the climate.
Halyard Point's mystery is caused by a problem unique to that one relay's own equipment.
The warming pattern explains Sable Flats, but Halyard Point's mystery remains unexplained.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: The colony's food supply cannot keep up.
That steady climb is the one pattern.
One station cannot see a planetary pattern.
It is why Halyard Point's spring keeps arriving earlier.

distractorRationale.1: This quote, on its own, only names the food-supply symptom.  The sentence right before it in the report is what ties that symptom to the warmer average, so the report connects the two directly even though this one line does not mention climate by itself.
distractorRationale.2: This sentence is about a single station's limited view of the wider pattern, not about any equipment problem at Halyard Point.
distractorRationale.3: The report calls the steady climb the one pattern underneath every local mystery this year has produced, which explicitly includes Halyard Point's, not just Sable Flats'.

items.explain: The synthesis draws the connection directly: a warmer average is why Halyard Point's spring keeps arriving earlier than the colony's food supply can follow, tying its local mystery to the same network-wide pattern explaining Sable Flats' dry years.  Each wrong choice tries to separate Halyard Point's mystery from that shared cause.

items.stem: Choose the three facts that together explain the colony's adaptation limit.
choices: The colony has stopped laying eggs earlier than April at all.
The colony's first-egg date has moved twenty-eight days earlier over thirty seasons.
The herring's arrival date has held close to the same date every season.
The fledge rate has climbed as the nesting date moved earlier.
The herring's arrival date has also moved twenty-eight days earlier, matching the terns.
The gap between nesting and the herring's arrival has grown wider each season.

distractorRationale.0: The thirtieth season's first eggs came on March tenth, before April even began, so the colony has not stopped laying eggs earlier than April.
distractorRationale.3: The fledge rate dropped from seventy-six percent in the first season to thirty-nine percent in the thirtieth, the opposite of climbing.
distractorRationale.4: The herring's arrival date has drifted by only about three days in either direction, nowhere close to the twenty-eight-day shift in the nesting date.

items.explain: The three correct facts trace the colony's actual adaptation limit: its nesting date shifted twenty-eight days earlier while the herring's own arrival date barely moved, so the gap between the two grew wider every season, which is exactly the mismatch the record's fledge-rate column tracks.  The three wrong choices each invert a number the record reports in the opposite direction.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that state what the fledge-rate column has actually been tracking all along.
spans: The gap between the two dates is what the fledge-rate column has been tracking.
It was never the nesting date by itself.
The colony is not nesting earlier by chance, since terns time their first eggs to the spring air and water.
The colony's chicks now hatch weeks before their food source even arrives.
items.explain: Both correct sentences state the record's own conclusion directly: the fledge-rate column tracks the growing gap between the two dates, not the nesting date on its own.  The other two sentences explain why the nesting date shifted and describe the consequence for the chicks, real details, but neither one is the record's own naming of what the column tracks.

items.stem: Tap the two sentences that describe a signal bouncing up and down rather than climbing steadily.
spans: Some years rose sharply.
One year barely rose at all.
Not one of the past ten years has dropped back.
That climb has stayed steady, year after year.
items.explain: Both correct sentences describe the temperature line's up-and-down bounce, some years rising sharply and other years barely rising at all, the pattern the report ties to short-term natural causes.  The other two sentences describe the carbon dioxide and fuel-use lines instead, which never drop back and climb by a steady amount every year.

items.stem: That {{0}} runs slower than the coastal air the terns respond to.

choices: clock
gap
mark

distractorRationale.1: The gap is the growing difference between the nesting date and the herring's arrival date, not the herring's own internal timing mechanism.
distractorRationale.2: The warm mark is the temperature threshold the terns respond to, a different animal's cue, not the herring's own ocean-temperature timing.

items.quote: That clock runs slower than the coastal air the terns respond to.
items.explain: The record names the herring's own ocean-temperature timing mechanism a clock, and states it runs slower than the coastal air signal the terns respond to, which is exactly why the two species' schedules have drifted apart.  Gap and mark each name a different piece of the record's own vocabulary, not the herring's timing mechanism itself.

items.stem: Over the thirty logged seasons, how did the herring's arrival date compare to the tern colony's nesting date?
choices: The herring's arrival date barely moved while the nesting date shifted twenty-eight days earlier.
Both dates shifted by almost exactly the same amount, staying in step with each other.
The herring's arrival date shifted earlier by even more than the nesting date did.
Neither date changed at all across the thirty seasons.

distractorRationale.1: The record reports a twenty-eight-day shift in the nesting date against only about a three-day drift in the herring's arrival date, far from matching each other.
distractorRationale.2: The record states the herring's arrival date has held near April twenty-first every season, drifting only about three days, nowhere close to the nesting date's twenty-eight-day shift.
distractorRationale.3: The nesting date moved from April seventh in the first season to March tenth in the thirtieth, a real and recorded twenty-eight-day change.

items.explain: The thirty-season record shows two very different clocks: the tern colony's first-egg date moved twenty-eight days earlier over thirty seasons, responding to warming spring air and water, while the herring's own ocean-temperature-driven arrival date held close to the same date, drifting only about three days either way, which is exactly why the gap between the two kept widening.

items.stem: A new instrument at a different station logs a number that rises sharply one year, drops the next, then rises again the year after.  Based on the synthesis report's own reasoning, what does this pattern most likely point to?
choices: A steady, human-linked cause, since any change at all over three years counts as the same kind of signal.
A short-term natural cause, since the number is bouncing up and down rather than climbing steadily.
An instrument malfunction, since real data should never rise and fall from year to year.
Nothing can be concluded from only three years of a new instrument's data.

distractorRationale.0: The report specifically distinguishes a bouncing signal from a steady one; a number that rises, drops, then rises again is bouncing, not climbing the same amount every year the way carbon dioxide and fuel use do.
distractorRationale.2: The report treats the temperature line's own up-and-down bounce as normal and expected, caused by ordinary short-term factors, not as evidence of broken equipment.
distractorRationale.3: The report does draw a conclusion from a bouncing pattern like this one: it treats that up-and-down shape itself as the signature of short-term natural causes, distinct from a steady climbing trend.

items.explain: Network Command's own rule distinguishes the two shapes directly: a signal that bounces up and down, some years rising sharply and other years barely moving, points to short-term natural causes, while only a signal that climbs by close to the same steady amount every year, without ever reversing, points to the network's ongoing, human-linked pattern.  A rise-drop-rise instrument reading matches the bouncing shape, not the steady one.

items.stem: According to the synthesis report, why can a single field station not see the network's full warming pattern on its own?
choices: A single station's instruments are never accurate enough to be trusted.
Network Command deliberately hides the combined data from individual stations.
A lone station can only see its own local report, not the pattern across every station and year together.
Each station's local mystery has nothing to do with any of the others.

distractorRationale.0: The report never questions any single station's instrument accuracy.  Its point is about scope, one report versus every station's reports together, not about accuracy.
distractorRationale.1: The report never describes Command withholding data.  It explains that the pattern only becomes visible once every station's separate reports are read side by side.
distractorRationale.3: The report's entire point is the opposite: every local mystery, Halyard Point's and Sable Flats', turns out to share the same underlying planetary cause once read together.

items.explain: The synthesis report states plainly that one station cannot see a planetary pattern and cannot see past its own single report, which is exactly why the pattern only becomes visible once the network reads every station's local mystery side by side, rather than any one relay's readings being unreliable or hidden.

items.stem: In eight words or fewer, name what the record shows chicks now do relative to their food source, the real cause behind the falling fledge rate.
accept: they hatch before the herring arrives
the chicks hatch before the herring
hatch before their food source arrives
hatch before the herring shows up
items.explain: The record's own closing description names the real cause directly: the colony's chicks now hatch weeks before the herring, their one food source, even arrive, a reversal from the colony's early seasons, when the herring were already there and settled in.  It was never simply the nesting date by itself that mattered.

partA.stem: Which proposal fails Command's constraint that the response must use only authority the Network already holds?
choices: Proposal C, since it depends on a fishery authority that does not answer to the Network.
Proposal A, since the Network has never run a feeding station before.
Proposal B, since fencing requires authority the Network does not have over its own land.
All three proposals fail this constraint equally.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: That authority covers its posts and the land around them.
The Network runs feeding stations at two other posts.
The fishery authority does not answer to the Network, though.
The authority to run one is not in question.

distractorRationale.1: This sentence says the Network already runs feeding stations at two other posts, which means it has done this before, not never.
distractorRationale.2: This sentence says the Network's own authority covers its posts and the land around them, exactly where fencing would go, so fencing does not require authority it lacks.
distractorRationale.3: This sentence says the authority question for Proposal A is not even in question, meaning it clearly passes, so the three proposals do not all fail equally.

items.explain: The report states plainly that the fishery authority does not answer to the Network, which means Proposal C would need cooperation from outside the Network's own authority, exactly the kind of authority Command's third constraint rules out.  The other choices each misread which proposal actually has that authority problem.

partA.stem: Proposal B fits Command's time and cost limits easily.  Why might it still fail to solve the colony's actual problem?
choices: The record shows chicks are starving during the food gap, a problem fencing against predators does not touch.
The fencing would cost far more than the field budget allows.
Fencing cannot be built within the one-season time limit Command set.
The Network lacks the authority to build fencing on its own land.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: That authority covers its posts and the land around them.
It can go up within days.
Fencing does nothing to touch that problem.
The fencing is inexpensive.

distractorRationale.1: This sentence says the fencing is inexpensive, the opposite of costing far more than the budget allows.
distractorRationale.2: This sentence says fencing can go up within days, well within any one-season time limit.
distractorRationale.3: This sentence says the Network's own authority covers its posts and the land around them, exactly where fencing would go.

items.explain: The report names the real weakness directly: the record shows chicks starving during the gap before the herring arrive, and fencing, which only keeps predators away from eggs and chicks, does nothing to touch that specific problem, even though it easily satisfies every one of Command's other constraints.  Each wrong choice invents a time, cost, or authority problem the report explicitly rules out.

partA.stem: An operative back at Sable Flats logs one unusually wet week and radios that the post's climate has changed.  What is the flaw in that call?
choices: One week of weather is not the same as a change in the long-term climate pattern averaged over years.
Sable Flats never receives rain of any kind, so the report must be a mistake.
Climate and weather mean exactly the same thing, so the call is correct.
The operative should have checked whether the wind belt shifted before saying anything.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Weather is what is happening outside the window this morning.
A single storm or a single clear week can happen at either station.
Climate is the pattern averaged over years.
These long-term patterns do not change because of one storm.

distractorRationale.1: This sentence says the opposite: long-term patterns do not change because of one storm, so a single storm cannot prove the climate itself has changed.
distractorRationale.2: This sentence defines weather narrowly, as what is happening outside the window this morning, a single moment, which the passage treats as different from climate, the pattern averaged over years.
distractorRationale.3: This sentence is about a single storm or clear week happening at a station, not about checking wind belts specifically, which the passage never suggests as a required step here.

items.explain: The passage draws the distinction directly: climate is the pattern averaged over years, while a single storm or a single clear week, exactly like the wet week the operative logged, can happen at either station without its long-term climate actually changing.  Each wrong choice either denies that distinction or invents a step the passage never asks for.

partA.stem: A new operative argues that this year's especially warm reading at one station is, by itself, solid proof of the network's warming pattern.  What is the flaw in that argument?
choices: A single year's temperature reading bounces naturally, so only the longer, steady trend across many stations and years actually counts as evidence.
Temperature readings are never reliable at any single station.
The warming pattern can only be proven using carbon dioxide data, never temperature.
One especially warm year always matches the carbon dioxide trend exactly.

partB.stem: Which sentence from the passage best supports the answer you just gave?
choices: Every station on the network logs its local temperature.
Every station's air-sampling equipment also logs atmospheric carbon dioxide.
A signal that bounces up and down, like the temperature line, usually points to short-term natural causes.
Some years rose sharply.

distractorRationale.1: This sentence says every station logs its own local temperature as a matter of course, which the network clearly treats as usable data, not something unreliable.
distractorRationale.2: This sentence says carbon dioxide is another number the network tracks, alongside temperature, not the only signal that can count as evidence.
distractorRationale.3: This sentence says some years rose sharply while others barely rose at all, which is exactly the bounce that does not match carbon dioxide's steady, unbroken climb.

items.explain: The synthesis explains why a single warm year is not solid proof: a signal that bounces up and down, like the temperature line, usually points to short-term natural causes, and only a steady climb across many years and every station, the way carbon dioxide and fuel use behave together, points to the network's real warming pattern.  Each wrong choice either dismisses temperature entirely or claims a match the passage does not support.

items.stem: Choose the three true facts about how the three proposals measure up against Command's constraints.
choices: Proposal A treats the survival gap each season instead of closing it for good.
Proposal A requires authority the Network does not currently have.
Proposal B is too expensive to fit inside this year's field budget.
Proposal B satisfies the time and cost limits but does not fix the actual food gap.
Proposal C could take longer than Command's one-season window to even be decided.
Proposal C is guaranteed to arrive before the chicks' hungriest stretch next season.

distractorRationale.1: The report says the authority to run a feeding station is not even in question, since the Network already runs two elsewhere.
distractorRationale.2: The report says the fencing itself is inexpensive, well inside the cost limit Command set.
distractorRationale.5: The report says no petition has ever been decided in under four months, well past the one-season window, so Proposal C is not guaranteed to arrive in time at all.

items.explain: The three correct facts summarize each proposal's real trade-off: Proposal A only treats the symptom each season, Proposal B is cheap and fast but does not fix the food gap, and Proposal C could take longer to decide than Command's own window allows.  The three wrong choices each invert a specific constraint the report states about a different proposal.

items.stem: Tap the three sentences that each state one of Command's named constraints on the response.
spans: That effect must appear within one nesting season.
Second, the response must cost less than this year's field budget for Halyard Point.
Third, the response must use only authority the Network already holds.
No emergency funding request is allowed.
The operative filing the final report must recommend one of three proposals.
items.explain: The three correct sentences each state one of Command's three named constraints directly: a one-season time limit, a cost limit tied to this year's budget, and a limit to authority the Network already holds.  The other two sentences add a supporting detail about emergency funding and describe the operative's overall task, neither one a constraint statement itself.

items.stem: Tap the three sentences, one for each proposal, that each name the specific reason that proposal falls short.
spans: It treats the survival gap each season rather than closing it.
Fencing does nothing to touch that problem.
The outcome does not lie inside the Network's authority.
Setup takes under two weeks.
It can go up within days.
items.explain: Each correct sentence names the specific reason one proposal falls short: Proposal A only treats the gap each season instead of closing it, Proposal B's fencing never touches the actual food-gap problem, and Proposal C's outcome sits outside the Network's own authority.  The other two sentences each describe a strength, fast setup, for a different proposal, not a flaw.

items.stem: Third, the response must use only {{0}} the Network already holds.

choices: time
budget
authority

distractorRationale.0: Time is the limit named in Command's first constraint, the one-season window, not the third constraint about what the Network is allowed to do.
distractorRationale.1: Budget is the limit named in Command's second constraint, the cost limit, not the third constraint about authority.

items.quote: Third, the response must use only authority the Network already holds.
items.explain: Command's third constraint names authority specifically, limiting the response to power the Network already holds rather than anything requiring an outside agency's cooperation.  Time and budget each name one of the other two constraints, the one-season window and the cost limit, not this third one.

items.stem: What is Command's FIRST constraint on the response, the one it states before cost or authority?
choices: The response must cost less than this year's field budget for Halyard Point.
The response must use only authority the Network already holds.
The response must be approved by the fishery authority before it can begin.
The response must show a real effect on chick survival within one nesting season.

distractorRationale.0: Command lists this as its second constraint, the cost limit, not the first one it names.
distractorRationale.1: Command lists this as its third constraint, the authority limit, not the first one it names.
distractorRationale.2: This is not one of Command's three named constraints at all; it is the specific obstacle facing Proposal C alone, not a general requirement Command set for every proposal.

items.explain: Command sets its constraints in a stated order, and the report names the time limit first: the response must show a real effect on chick survival within one nesting season, before it goes on to state the cost limit second and the authority limit third.

items.stem: Suppose a fourth proposal called for the Network to seek new region-wide fishery regulation that would move the herring season's start date permanently.  Based on the report's own reasoning about Proposal C, would this new idea likely satisfy Command's authority constraint?
choices: No, since it would still depend on a fishery authority that does not answer to the Network, the same problem Proposal C already has.
Yes, since a permanent regulation change is always more powerful than a one-time petition.
Yes, since region-wide regulation falls outside any single fishery authority's control.
There is no way to know without more information about the fishery authority.

distractorRationale.1: The permanence of the change does not touch the actual constraint.  The report's problem with Proposal C is which authority controls the decision, not how long the decision would last.
distractorRationale.2: The report describes the fishery authority as the body that decides herring-season timing.  A region-wide version of that same request would still need that same authority's approval, not less of it.
distractorRationale.3: The report already gives the needed information: the fishery authority does not answer to the Network and no petition has ever been decided in under four months, both of which apply just as directly to a bigger, region-wide version of the same request.

items.explain: The report's actual objection to Proposal C is that the fishery authority does not answer to the Network and could take months longer than Command's one-season window to decide, a problem tied to WHO controls the decision, not to the size or permanence of what is being asked for, so a bigger regional version of the same request would run into the identical authority and timing problem.

items.stem: The colony's survival problem began as a shift in the terns' own nesting timing, driven by warming spring air, and it eventually showed up as a falling fledge rate in the chicks.  Using the field manual's own vocabulary, which word best names the way a change in one part led to a change in a different, connected part?
choices: component
interaction
system
subsystem

distractorRationale.0: Component names one small physical part, not the connection between a timing shift in one species and a survival change in another.
distractorRationale.2: System names a whole set of parts working toward one job, not the specific ripple connecting one change to another.
distractorRationale.3: Subsystem names one smaller system nested inside a bigger one, not the event of one part's change causing a connected part to change too.

items.explain: The field manual defines an interaction as what happens when one part changes and a connected part changes with it, exactly the shape of the colony's own mystery: the terns' own nesting timing shifted twenty-eight days earlier, driven by warming spring air, and that shift rippled into the chicks' widening food gap and falling fledge rate, the same vocabulary word tile one introduces on a station's own life-support system.

items.stem: In eight words or fewer, name the one proposal that both fits every one of Command's constraints and actually treats the chicks' food gap.
accept: proposal a, the temporary feeding station
items.explain: Proposal A fits inside Command's time and cost limits and needs no new authority, and unlike Proposal B, it directly targets the chicks' actual problem, the food gap the nesting record identified, by stocking fish through the exact three-week window before the herring arrive, even though it must be repeated each season rather than closing the gap for good.
